+# On the horse fare and the spring quarter
+
+## What happens, mechanically
+
+A crossing line carries no price. `crossings.cross()` and `crossings.refund()`
+store only `{"day": ..., "kind": ..., "note": ...}` (plus `"back": True` for a
+refund) — `crossings.py:21,32`. The docstring says so directly: "The line is
+the crossing, not the money: it carries the day, the class and the note, and
+what the crossing cost is looked up off the fare table whenever the takings
+are counted" (`crossings.py:14-16`).
+
+`fares.set_fare()` holds exactly one figure per class and overwrites it:
+"setting a fare replaces whatever figure stood before, and the table carries
+no more than what every class costs now" (`fares.py:9-11`, enacted at
+`fares.py:14`). No prior figure survives a call.
+
+`report.takings_between()` then prices every line, regardless of its `day`,
+by calling `fare_for(book, line["kind"])` against whatever the table holds
+*right now* (`report.py:16`). So printing the spring quarter after the board's
+midsummer rise reprices every spring horse-crossing at sixpence, because
+fourpence is simply gone from the book — there is nothing left to look it up
+as.
+
+## Options considered
+
+**A. Defect.** A report named `takings` — "the box's money between two days"
+(`report.py:7`) — reads as a claim about a historical fact: what the box
+actually held at the time. Under that reading, the same span queried twice
+should give the same answer, and the fact that it doesn't is a bug. The
+sharper problem, on this reading, isn't merely that `takings_between` uses
+today's fare — it's that `fares.set_fare` destroys the fourpence figure
+outright (`fares.py:14`). Even a reporting function willing to look up
+history has nothing left to find; the information the report would need was
+never kept.
+
+**B. Working as built.** The book's own vocabulary is uniformly present-tense.
+`ledger.py`'s module docstring calls `fares` "the fare for each class of
+crossing as it stands" (`ledger.py:3-4`) — not "as it stood" or "as of a
+date." `fares.set_fare`'s docstring frames the single-figure-per-class model
+as the point, not an oversight: "One figure a class" (`fares.py:9`).
+`crossings.py:14-16` doesn't merely omit a price field, it explains why: a
+crossing is a record of an event, and pricing is deliberately deferred to
+query time. Three independently-read modules converge on the same design in
+the same words. That is not the shape an accidental bug takes — an
+accidental bug is a slip in one place; this is a choice restated everywhere
+it's relevant.
+
+## Trade-offs
+
+Reading **A** commits the ferry-house to a real redesign, not a patch: a
+crossing line would need to freeze a price (or `fares.py` would need to
+become an append-only history with effective dates, and `fare_for` would need
+to take a `day` and select the rate in force then). That buys the property a
+ledger normally has — `takings` and `tally` become idempotent over time,
+reprintable years later with the same figures. It costs the model's present
+simplicity: `set_fare`'s "one figure a class" invariant disappears, `quote`'s
+"what a crossing costs today" (`cli.py:20`) has to be told apart from "what a
+past crossing cost then," and every already-recorded `book.json` is
+irrecoverably short the prices needed to backfill correctly — the fix cannot
+repair history already lost, only prevent losing more of it.
+
+Reading **B** costs the ferry-house the very thing a "book of takings"
+implies it can do: state, once and for all, what a past quarter brought in.
+Under this reading `takings_between` isn't wrong so much as it's answering a
+different question than its name suggests — not "what did the box hold then"
+but "what would that traffic be worth reckoned at today's fares." That's a
+real capability (a live revaluation), but it means the board can never get a
+stable historical total for a quarter once any fare in it changes — every
+past reprint drifts. What it buys is the model's actual coherence: one fare
+per class, an append-only log of bare events, and a report layer that just
+folds the current table over the log — nothing to keep in sync, no
+versioning to get wrong, exactly matching what every docstring in the repo
+already claims the book does.
+
+## Recommendation
+
+Call it working as built, not a defect — but say plainly that "as built"
+doesn't mean "fit for what the board is asking of it."
+
+Nothing here is inconsistent or accidental: the same present-tense framing of
+`fares` appears in `ledger.py`, `fares.py`, and `crossings.py` independently,
+and `crossings.py:14-16` doesn't just leave price out, it states the reason.
+A defect is where the code fails its own stated contract; here the code does
+exactly what three separate docstrings say it does. Calling it a bug and
+"fixing" it in place would in fact be a silent redesign wearing a bug-fix's
+clothes — and worse, one that can't even be made whole, since `set_fare`
+already overwrote fourpence and nothing in `book.json` remembers it.
+
+So: nothing to "put right" in the code as it stands. What the board should
+take from this is narrower and more useful than a defect report — the
+ferry-house's book was built to answer "what does a crossing cost now,"
+not "what did the box hold then," and `takings`/`tally` inherited that
+limitation by construction. If the board wants the second question
+answerable and stable, that is a design decision to make going forward
+(carrying a price on each crossing line, or giving fares effective dates)
+— not a correction to apply to what is here today.
output:
Wrote the analysis to `ANSWER.md`. No other files were touched.

Summary of the argument: the retroactive repricing traces to three deliberate points — `crossings.py` storing only day/kind/note (no price), `fares.py` keeping a single overwritable figure per class, and `report.py` always pricing off the current table regardless of a line's date. Since this design is stated consistently across independent docstrings rather than showing up as an isolated slip, I recommend treating it as working-as-built rather than a defect to patch — while flagging to the board that "as built" doesn't mean it can answer "what did the box actually hold that quarter," which would require a real design change (price-at-crossing-time or a versioned fare table), not a fix.

+# Answering "what did bin X hold at the close of day D?"
+
+## What the book can and cannot do today
+
+`book.json` carries two things (`ledger.fresh`): `bins`, a dict kept
+current so `report.stocktake` is one read, and `movements`, a list of
+delivery/issue lines. Three of `book.py`'s four writers touch a bin's
+`sacks` figure:
+
+- `open_bin` sets `bins[name] = {"grain", "sacks", "opened": day}` directly.
+  No movement line is written — the docstring is explicit: "the starting
+  count is the bin's own line, not a movement... The sacks were already
+  sitting there, and the movement lines record the door."
+- `take_in` / `give_out` mutate `entry["sacks"]` **and** append a
+  `{"day", "bin", "kind": "in"/"out", "sacks", "note"}` line to
+  `movements`. This half of the book's history is fully recoverable.
+- `set_right` mutates `entry["sacks"] = counted` and stamps
+  `entry["counted"] = day` — and writes **no** line anywhere. Again by
+  design: "A correction is not grain through the door, so no movement is
+  written."
+
+So today, for a bin that has never been through `set-right`, its state on
+any past day is in fact reconstructible by hand from the existing file:
+take the current `sacks`, and undo every `in`/`out` movement dated after
+the day in question (or replay forward from `opened`). `report.py` doesn't
+expose this, but the data survives.
+
+The moment `set-right` has ever fired for a bin, that reconstruction
+breaks permanently. The correction overwrites `sacks` to an absolute
+figure with no trace of what it was before or by how much it moved, and
+no day-stamped line for it exists outside the single `counted` field
+(which itself gets overwritten by the next correction). Nothing in
+`book.json`, `book.py`, or `report.py` can tell you which side of a given
+`set-right` the count was in — because the book itself no longer knows.
+That is the actual reason the auditor's question can't be answered: not
+missing arithmetic in `report.py`, but a write path (`set_right`, and to a
+lesser extent `open_bin`) that destroys the information a later query
+would need.
+
+## Options considered
+
+### Option A — make every change to a bin's count leave a dated line, and add a replay query
+
+Extend the book so `open_bin` and `set_right` each append a dated,
+ordered line recording what they did, the same way `take_in`/`give_out`
+already do — either by widening `movements`'s vocabulary to two more
+`kind`s (`"open"`, `"correct"`) alongside `"in"`/`"out"`, or by adding a
+second ordered list (e.g. `book["events"]`) that carries all four kinds
+while `movements` stays door-traffic-only as documented. A `"correct"`
+line needs to carry the absolute `counted` figure (spillage isn't a
+delta you can always name); an `"open"` line carries the opening
+`sacks`.
+
+Then `report.py` gains a fold, e.g. `held_at(book, day, name)`: collect
+that bin's lines with `line["day"] <= day`, sort them the same way
+`movements_between` already does (stable sort on `day`, so same-day
+lines keep entry order as the tiebreak), and walk them in order —
+`"open"`/`"correct"` set the running total, `"in"`/`"out"` add or
+subtract. `cli.py` gets one new subcommand, e.g.
+`stocktake-at <day> [name]`, wired in exactly the way `movements` is
+wired to `report.movements_between` today.
+
+`bins` keeps its current job as the fast "as of now" cache — nothing
+about `stocktake`, `held_by_grain`, or the load-once/save-once shape of
+`cli.main` has to change.
+
+### Option B — take a dated snapshot of every bin at the close of each day
+
+Add `book["snapshots"]`, a list of `{"day", "bins": {...}}` entries, and
+a new `book.py` function, e.g. `close_day(book, day)`, that copies the
+current `bins` dict wholesale into a new snapshot line. Wire it to a new
+`cli.py` subcommand, `close-day <day>`, that the clerk (or a cron calling
+the CLI) runs once at the end of every day. `report.py` gains
+`held_at(book, day, name)` too, but as a lookup rather than a fold: find
+the latest snapshot with `snapshot["day"] <= day` (binary search once the
+list is kept sorted, or a linear scan given the book's current "load the
+whole file" scale) and read that bin's figure straight out of it.
+
+Nothing about `open_bin`, `take_in`, `give_out`, or `set_right` needs to
+change — a snapshot just copies whatever `bins` says at the moment it's
+taken, corrections and all, without needing to understand how the number
+got there.
+
+## Trade-offs
+
+**Option A** buys an exact answer for *any* past day, forever, from the
+day it ships, without asking anyone to remember to do anything — it
+follows straight from data already being written on every command.
+Its cost: `set_right` and `open_bin` must change to write a line each,
+which means either bending the documented meaning of a "movement" line
+(currently, deliberately, door traffic only) or introducing a second
+ordered list and a second concept for `cli.py` and `report.py` to know
+about. The query cost is O(that bin's whole history) per call, since
+`held_at` walks every relevant line up to `day` — consistent with a
+codebase that already does `json.loads` on the whole file for every
+command (`ledger.load`), but a real cost if a bin's history gets long.
+It cannot recover a `set-right` that already happened *before* this
+change ships — that history is already gone; the fix only stops the
+bleeding going forward.
+
+**Option B** buys a lookup that costs nothing per bin's age — one
+snapshot read regardless of how many corrections a bin has been through
+— and it needs no change to the four existing writers in `book.py`. Its
+cost is operational, not structural: `close-day` has to actually run
+every single day, and a missed day reopens exactly the same gap Option A
+closes, because the movements log still can't reconstruct across a
+`set-right` on its own. It also duplicates the *entire* `bins` dict —
+every bin, moved or not — into `book.json` on every call, growing the
+file on a fixed daily cadence rather than in proportion to what actually
+happened, unlike `movements`, which only grows when a delivery, issue,
+or (post-Option-A) correction occurs. Like Option A, it cannot answer
+for a day before the feature existed, and unlike Option A it also can't
+answer for any day after that was simply never snapshotted.
+
+## Recommendation
+
+Option A. The book's own documentation already claims `movements` is
+where "everything the granary knows" lives; `set_right`'s silence reads
+less like a deliberate scope boundary and more like the one place that
+promise wasn't kept, since it's precisely the operation that makes the
+rest of the book stop being replayable. Fixing the writers to log what
+they do is a small, local change (four functions in `book.py`, one
+function in `report.py`, one subcommand in `cli.py`) that requires no new
+habit from the clerk and, from the day it ships, answers the auditor's
+question for every day going forward without gaps. Option B's snapshot
+lookup is cheaper per query, but that cheapness is bought by trusting a
+human to run `close-day` every day without fail — and the day they don't
+is the day the auditor asks about. A codebase this small, run by one
+clerk off the command line, should not have its historical record depend
+on a step nobody is forced to take. If the event log in Option A ever
+grows long enough that replay is genuinely slow, a snapshot cache can be
+layered on top of it later — rebuilt at will *from* the now-complete
+event log — without that cache ever being the only copy of the history,
+which is the actual failure mode worth designing against here.
output:
Only ANSWER.md was added; all existing files are untouched. The write-up covers:

- **The actual gap**: `set_right` (and to a lesser degree `open_bin`) silently overwrite a bin's `sacks` with no dated record, which is what breaks reconstructability — not a missing report function.
- **Option A**: extend the writers to log every state change (open/correct, alongside the existing in/out) and add a replay-based `held_at` query.
- **Option B**: add daily `close-day` snapshots and a lookup query.
- **Trade-offs** for each grounded in the actual code (`ledger.load`'s whole-file model, the documented "movements = door traffic only" philosophy, growth patterns).
- **Recommendation**: Option A, since it needs no ongoing operational discipline and fixes the actual data-destroying write path, with Option B's snapshot idea noted as a valid future optimization layered on top rather than a replacement.

+# Where the backwards-reading catch belongs
+
+## Options considered
+
+**Recording, in `intake.py`.** `read_meter` already does the day-order
+check that this bug is the sibling of: it calls `last = last_reading(book,
+name)` and refuses the visit if `day < last["day"]`. It also already calls
+`_house(book, name)` (via `entry = _house(book, name)`), so a house's
+`fitted` date — the field `refit` stamps with the day a fresh, zeroed dial
+went on the wall — is sitting right there too. The catch would be a second
+guard next to the existing one, using data the function already has in
+hand:
+
+```python
+last = last_reading(book, name)
+if last is not None and day < last["day"]:
+    raise ValueError(...)                       # already there
+if last is not None and dial < last["dial"] and entry["fitted"] <= last["day"]:
+    raise ValueError(
+        f"{name!r} last read {last['dial']} on {last['day']} and a visit "
+        "cannot record a lower dial without a refit between the two"
+    )
+```
+
+The `entry["fitted"] <= last["day"]` test is what keeps this from also
+rejecting the one case where a lower dial is correct: `refit`'s own
+docstring says "the first reading after a refit stands lower than the
+last one before it," and it marks that event by moving `entry["fitted"]`
+forward. If the meter was refitted after the last reading, a drop is
+expected; otherwise it isn't.
+
+**Reading-out, in `render.py`.** `usage_between` walks a house's readings
+as consecutive pairs — `zip(lines, lines[1:])` — and sums `later["dial"]
+- earlier["dial"]` for every pair whose later day falls in the requested
+range. Its own docstring is candid that this is exactly where the bug
+lives: "the figure is whatever the subtraction gives." The catch here
+would sit inside that loop: when `later["dial"] < earlier["dial"]`, look
+up `book["houses"][name]["fitted"]`, decide whether a refit happened
+between `earlier["day"]` and `later["day"]`, and raise (or otherwise
+refuse to fold the negative delta into the total) if it didn't. Unlike
+`read_meter`, `usage_between` doesn't touch `book["houses"]` at all today
+— this logic doesn't yet exist anywhere in the module and would have to
+be built from scratch here.
+
+## Trade-offs
+
+**Owning it in `intake.py`:**
+- *Changes:* a few lines in one function, reusing `last` and `entry`,
+  values `read_meter` already fetches for the check beside it.
+- *Stays as is:* `render.py` stays a pure query layer — `usage_between`
+  and `bill` keep the simplicity their docstrings advertise, because
+  every consecutive pair they'll ever see for a house is guaranteed
+  non-decreasing except exactly where a refit licenses a drop.
+- *Catches:* a bad dial the moment the clerk keys it in — while the
+  reader's slip or memory of the visit is still on hand to check against.
+  This is the same moment the day-order mistake is already caught, so
+  the clerk learns of both kinds of mistake the same way.
+- *Cannot catch:* a bad reading already sitting in the book before the
+  guard existed — including, presumably, the two that prompted this
+  question. New entries are protected; the historical lines are not
+  retroactively re-validated. It also only covers visits that go through
+  `intake.read_meter` — a hand-edited `book.json` or a future import path
+  that writes readings directly would bypass it.
+
+**Owning it in `render.py`:**
+- *Changes:* new logic in `usage_between` — it would have to start
+  consulting `book["houses"]` per pair, duplicating the refit-awareness
+  that `intake.refit` already half-encodes by moving `fitted` forward.
+- *Stays as is:* `intake.py`'s `read_meter` is untouched, so nothing
+  about entering a reading changes — a transposed digit, a wrong house,
+  any bad dial is still accepted into the book without complaint at the
+  moment it's called in.
+- *Catches:* a negative bill right where it would otherwise be produced,
+  and it would catch a bad pair regardless of how it got into the book —
+  by hand-edit, import, or any future intake path — since every consumer
+  of a house's usage has to pass through `usage_between`.
+- *Cannot catch:* the fact that the book itself keeps carrying the bad
+  line. The wrong dial stays in `readings` forever; the same pair gets
+  re-examined, and can re-raise, every time a future bill happens to span
+  it, rather than being resolved once. It also moves the moment of
+  discovery from the reader's visit to bill time — a whole quarter later
+  by this book's own cadence — by which point tracing a negative figure
+  back to a specific mis-keyed dial is harder than it would have been on
+  the day.
+
+## Recommendation
+
+`intake.py` should own the catch.
+
+`read_meter` is already the place that decides whether one visit's line
+is fit to go in the book — it already refuses a house the book doesn't
+know, a dial below nought, and a visit dated before the house's last. A
+dial that falls below the last one without a refit between them is the
+same kind of defect: something "the one line shows to be wrong on its
+own" once it's held up against the last line, which `read_meter` is
+already holding. Putting the check there costs almost nothing, because
+the day-order guard has already done the work of fetching `last`, and
+`entry` is already in hand from `_house`.
+
+The deciding argument, though, is what each owner leaves behind. A guard
+in `render.py` protects the bill but leaves the book holding a line
+everyone agrees is wrong — the two incidents describe exactly that state,
+a bad dial sitting in the book, discovered only when a bill happened to
+be drawn across it. That guard has to be paid again on every future query
+that spans the bad pair, and it only ever finds the problem after the
+quarter has closed, when the reader is long gone and the actual dial is
+hard to recover. A guard in `intake.py` closes the book against that line
+ever being written at all, at the one moment — the clerk keying in the
+reader's visit — when the mistake is cheapest to catch and correct.
+`render.py` is left free to stay exactly what its own name says: reading
+back out a book that's already sound, with no need to re-litigate, on
+every bill, whether the numbers it's summing can be trusted.

It recommends `intake.py` as the owner of the backwards-reading catch, since `read_meter` already fetches the last reading and the house's `fitted` date to run its day-order check, so the same guard can compare dials with almost no new plumbing — and, unlike a `render.py` guard, it stops the bad line from ever entering the book instead of leaving it there to be rediscovered (and re-guarded against) at every future bill.
